items.title: Real-world trajectories in psoriatic arthritis under risankizumab therapy.
items.abstract: Risankizumab, a selective IL-23p19 inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy in randomized clinical trials, but real-world data remain limited. To evaluate the real-world effectiveness and safety of risankizumab in PsA, and to identify baseline predictors of treatment response. This multicentre, retrospective, longitudinal, real-world study included 112 PsA patients fulfilling the CASPAR criteria enrolled across seven Italian combined dermato-rheumatology centers. DAPSA and other longitudinal variables were assessed at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months. Patients were stratified as D2T (risankizumab as ≥3 rd -line biologic therapy) or nD2T, and as responders (DAPSA≤14) or non-responders at 6 months. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify baseline predictors of DAPSA response. Risankizumab induced rapid and sustained improvement across PsA domains. A significant DAPSA reduction was observed (p<0.001), with 62.5% and 69% of evaluable patients achieving DAPSA response at 6 and 12 months, respectively. D2T patients exhibited higher baseline disease activity and burden but achieved comparable disease control by month 12. In multivariable analysis, higher baseline VAS pain was independently associated with lower odds of DAPSA response at 6 months (OR 0.74; 95% CI 0.55-0.96). Treatment persistence at 12 months was 82.1%. Adverse events were infrequent (4.5%), and only one led to treatment discontinuation. Risankizumab demonstrated real-world effectiveness and tolerability across heterogeneous PsA trajectories, including multi-failure patients. Higher baseline pain was independently associated with lower odds of achieving DAPSA remission/low disease activity, highlighting the importance of pain assessment in treatment stratification and supporting further studies on inflammatory and non-inflammatory determinants of response. Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term inflammatory disease that can affect the joints, skin and other parts of the body. Some people do not respond well to several treatments and can be difficult to treat. Risankizumab is a medicine that blocks part of the immune system involved in inflammation, but information on how it works in everyday clinical practice is still limited. In this study, we reviewed the medical records of 112 people with psoriatic arthritis treated with risankizumab in several Italian centres. We assessed disease activity before treatment and after 3, 6 and 12 months. We also compared patients who had already received several previous biologic treatments with those treated earlier in their disease course. Overall, risankizumab was associated with rapid and sustained improvement. Among patients with available data at 12 months, 69% reached remission or low disease activity. Patients who had already failed several previous biologic treatments had more severe disease at the start, but by 12 months their level of disease control was similar to that of other patients. We also found that patients reporting higher pain levels before starting risankizumab were less likely to reach good disease control after 6 months. This suggests that pain assessment may help doctors better understand which patients are most likely to benefit from treatment, and that both inflammatory and non-inflammatory causes of pain should be considered. Most patients continued risankizumab after 12 months. Side effects were uncommon, and only one patient stopped treatment because of an adverse event. Overall, these findings support risankizumab as an effective and well-tolerated option in real-world psoriatic arthritis care, including in patients with more complex treatment histories.

items.title: Novel machine learning models including adipose-muscle indices for the prediction of musculoskeletal complications in rheumatoid arthritis: A cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: This research aimed to investigate the associations of multiple adipose-muscle indices with secondary osteoporosis (OP) and sarcopenia in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. To develop a comprehensive early diagnostic model for musculoskeletal loss in RA patients based on non-invasive adipose-muscle indices. A cross-sectional and Mendelian randomization (MR) study. Fourteen machine learning (ML) algorithms were applied to select features from 33 candidate variables and were incorporated to construct clinical predictive models for OP, sarcopenia, and osteo-sarcopenia (OS). Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis explored dose-response relationships. MR methods were used to analyze potential causal effects. Six key features were identified, of which the fat-to-muscle ratio (FMR) and the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio (SVR) were the most prominent. FMR was a risk factor for OP, whereas SVR was a protective factor against sarcopenia. The LightGBM model demonstrated superior performance in predicting OS (AUC = 0.988). MR analysis further indicated that body fat mass fully mediated the causal pathway from RA to OP and sarcopenia. ML models based on hybrid adipose-muscle indices demonstrated exceptional predictive value for subclinical musculoskeletal loss in RA patients.

items.title: Deciphering the molecular mechanisms linking abnormal mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to myeloid cell activation in systemic lupus erythematosus through multi-scale transcriptomics.
items.abstract: Abnormal mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC) activity is a pivotal driver in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, the molecular mechanisms linking it to immune phenotypes and disease progression remain unclear. This study aims to systematically determine core biomarkers of MRC dysfunction in SLE and explore their potential pathogenic mechanisms through multi-scale transcriptomic analysis. Five bulk transcriptomic series from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were integrated to screen for differentially expressed genes linked to MRC abnormalities. Three machine learning algorithms and SHAP analysis were applied to identify core signature genes. Leveraging these markers, a diagnostic model was developed, along with constructing molecular interaction and regulatory networks. We elucidated the biological functions through functional enrichment, immune infiltration analyzes, and correlation analysis with key therapeutic targets. Furthermore, we integrated three single-cell datasets and applied Seurat clustering, pseudotime analysis, and CellChat to characterize the expression patterns, differentiation trajectories, and interaction networks of core genes within specific cell subpopulations. Our results identified 18 biomarkers, with SCO2 emerging as the primary core gene. The diagnostic model achieved high discriminatory accuracy. Multi-dimensional functional analyzes uncovered a potential role for SCO2 bridging mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction with antiviral innate immune activation. Single-cell analysis localized SCO2 overexpression primarily to monocytes and dendritic cells, showing a downregulation trajectory during myeloid differentiation. We found that SCO2 + myeloid cells exhibit altered interaction networks within the immune microenvironment, characterized by enriched MHC-I/II and MIF signaling. In conclusion, SCO2 is a critical biomarker of MRC activity in SLE, reflecting the mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming that drives immune dysregulation.

items.title: MRI-assessed structural damage progression in sacroiliac joints of European routine care patients with axial spondyloarthritis receiving biological or conventional therapy.
items.abstract: To describe progression of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-detected sacroiliac joint (SIJ) structural lesions in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) in routine care. Bionaïve patients with axSpA from 5 European countries were included if a follow-up SIJ MRI was available 1 to 4 years after baseline. MRIs were centrally assessed using the Spondyloarthritis Research Consortium of Canada SIJ scoring systems by readers blinded to chronology. Patients were stratified by initiation of biological therapy during follow-up. Structural progression was described and compared. Of 179 patients, 122 had a first MRI indicative of SpA. In these patients, baseline scores for bone marrow oedema (BME), fat lesions, and erosions were significantly higher in those initiating biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) (n = 53) than in conventionally treated patients (n = 59). The MRI interval was 1.8 years in bDMARD-treated patients and 2.3 years in conventionally treated patients. In bDMARD-treated patients, mean Spondyloarthritis Research Consortium of Canada changes during MRI follow-up were BME -14.7, fat lesions +1.2, erosions -2.4, backfill +1.6, and ankylosis +0.2. Corresponding changes in conventionally treated patients were -3.0, +0.03, -0.04, +0.9, and +0.7. Ankylosis progression occurred in 15% of conventionally treated patients and 9% of those receiving bDMARDs. Backfill and ankylosis at baseline correlated with ankylosis progression in conventionally treated patients (Spearman's ρ = 0.38 and 0.42) but not in bDMARD-treated patients (ρ = -0.17 and 0.09). Erosions decreased only with bDMARD therapy. Baseline backfill was associated with ankylosis progression in conventional but not bDMARD-treated patients, suggesting a potential dissociation between backfill and ankylosis under biologics. Future studies should assess causality.

items.title: Histone lactylation in fibroblast-like synoviocytes drives CXCL1-mediated immune cell recruitment in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) drive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) progression by recruiting immune cells. Metabolic reprogramming, marked by enhanced glycolysis and lactate accumulation, contributes to RA pathogenesis. Here, an analysis of a public metabolomics dataset identified elevated plasma lactate in patients with RA. Histone lactylation was increased in synovial FLS from patients with RA and was linked to upregulated expression of the chemokine CXCL1 and enhanced immune cell recruitment. In collagen-induced arthritis and SKG mouse models, prophylactic CXCL1 neutralization or lactate dehydrogenase inhibition reduced immune cell infiltration, alleviated joint inflammation, and mitigated bone destruction. Lactate dehydrogenase inhibition also reduced synovial lactate levels, histone lactylation, and CXCL1 expression. These findings support a role for histone lactylation in FLS-mediated immune cell recruitment and suggest that this pathway warrants further investigation as a therapeutic target in RA.

items.title: Spatial transcriptomic mapping of anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis reveals perivascular enrichment of type I interferon responses and immune activation.
items.abstract: Anti-MDA5 autoantibody-positive dermatomyositis (MDA5+ DM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy associated with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease and a high mortality rate, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. To investigate this, we profiled the spatial transcriptome of muscle tissues from healthy controls, MDA5+, and MDA5- patients. We found that MDA5+ muscles exhibit a distinct spatial transcriptomic architecture driven by profound microenvironmental remodeling, accompanied by focal immune infiltration. Crucially, spatial niche analysis revealed that the type I interferon (IFN-I) signature is highly enriched within the endothelial cell (EC) niche. This perivascular niche also displayed enriched TGF-β, NF-κB, hypoxia, and TNF-α signaling, alongside transcriptomic signatures indicative of heightened inflammation and compromised oxygen transport. Altogether, our results characterize the distinct vascular pathology of MDA5+ DM muscles and provide a spatial mechanistic rationale for targeting these perivascular inflammatory pathways.

items.title: NLRP3 genetic variation and haplotype patterns in Iraqi Kurdish adults with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and healthy controls: a case-control study.
items.abstract: Whether inherited NLRP3 variation contributes to rheumatoid arthritis (RA) susceptibility remains uncertain. We examined associations of NLRP3-region genotypes, alleles, and four-locus haplotypes with physician-classified seropositive RA in Iraqi Kurdish adults. This hospital-based case-control genetic substudy included 50 patients with physician-classified seropositive RA and 50 healthy controls. Bidirectional Sanger sequencing assessed rs2527241787, rs3806265, chr1:247,423,076, and rs10754558. Genotype, allele, inheritance model, linkage disequilibrium, and estimated four-locus haplotype analyses were performed. Reported genetic odds ratios were unadjusted; Benjamini-Hochberg correction covered 15 estimable inheritance model tests. No individual variant showed a robust association with RA. A nominal recessive association for chr1:247,423,076 AA (odds ratio 3.50, 95% confidence interval 1.15-10.63; P = 0.040) did not persist after correction (adjusted P = 0.600). The global four-locus haplotype comparison was P = 0.0065, with nominal differences for TAAC (8.9% vs. 1.2% in cases and controls; odds ratio 8.22, P = 0.018) and TATC (11.6% vs 23.7%; odds ratio 0.42, P = 0.042). rs2527241787 departed from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in both groups. The exploratory haplotype differences require independent replication. The small sample, Hardy-Weinberg departure, and unadjusted association estimates limit inference; these findings neither exclude a role for NLRP3 in RA nor support changes to clinical genetic testing, diagnosis, or treatment. Key Points • No individual NLRP3-region variant showed a robust association with rheumatoid arthritis in this cohort. • The global four-locus haplotype comparison yielded a nominal difference between cases and controls. • Small sample size, Hardy-Weinberg departure, and unadjusted estimates make the genetic findings exploratory. • The results do not support a change in clinical testing or care and require independent replication.

items.title: Decoding treatment non-response in spondyloarthritis.
items.abstract: The term spondyloarthritis refers to a spectrum of inflammatory diseases, including axial spondyloarthritis and psoriatic arthritis, in which musculoskeletal and extra-musculoskeletal manifestations coexist. Targeted therapies have improved outcomes, yet many patients achieve only a partial response and sustained remission remains uncommon, irrespective of the drug mode of action used. Observations of repeated treatment failures have given rise to the concepts of difficult-to-manage and treatment-refractory disease, but non-response itself is inconsistently defined and is often treated as a single phenomenon. However, treatment non-response is a heterogeneous construct that needs to be unravelled by first differentiating apparent from true non-response. Four distinct clinical patterns of true non-response can be identified - primary non-response, secondary loss of response, divergent responses across disease domains and paradoxical reactions - shaped to differing extents by drug exposure, dependence on the targeted pathway and anatomical compartmentalization. Recognizing these patterns and likely mechanistic underpinnings could support more rational treatment selection, limit unnecessary switching of targeted therapies and inform future biomarker-driven strategies to anticipate and ultimately prevent non-response.

items.title: The pathogenesis of systemic manifestations in Sjögren disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren disease (SjD) is a common and chronic autoimmune systemic disease characterized by dryness, fatigue, pain and possible organ dysfunction. Understanding of SjD remains largely centred on the salivary glands, given that approximately 90% of patients report xerostomia and the glands are routinely sampled for diagnosis. However, SjD is a highly heterogeneous disease, and most patients present with systemic (extra-glandular) involvement at diagnosis, including interstitial lung disease, arthritis and renal disease. T cells seem central to the development of organ-specific disease, whereas B cells are pivotal to autoantibody production and lymphomagenesis. Several areas of uncertainty remain, including why certain organs are targeted by inflammation, understanding the disconnect between symptoms and pathology, and whether targeting the T cell-predominant infiltrate might have therapeutic benefit. Therefore, the pathogenesis of SjD might be best explained as a continuum of inflammation extending from the glands to distant target organs. A deeper understanding of SjD pathogenesis will be instrumental in the development of targeted therapies in organ-threatening disease.

items.title: Mechanisms bridging autoimmunity and autoinflammation in axial spondyloarthritis: current evidence and translational implications.
items.abstract: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) illustrates the limitations of classifying immune-mediated diseases as strictly autoimmune or autoinflammatory. Its strong association with HLA-B27 and epistatic interaction with endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1) support a contribution from adaptive immunity through altered antigen processing and presentation. At the same time, axSpA lacks high-titre, disease-defining autoantibodies and preferentially affects mechanically loaded sites, including the entheses and sacroiliac joints. Mucosal barrier dysfunction, innate and stromal responses, and IL-17A production by several lymphocyte populations are also implicated. However, findings from blood, peripheral synovium, gut, ligament and non-inflamed enthesis cannot be assumed to represent the same axial lesion. This critical narrative review examines how adaptive, innate and stromal processes may interact in axSpA. "Bridging mechanism" is used as a working term for a directional and testable relationship across an adaptive-innate immunity or immune-stromal boundary, anchored to a defined phenotype, tissue and study system. It does not replace the established autoimmune-autoinflammatory continuum or MHC-I-opathy concepts. Evidence remains uneven. HLA-B27-related stress and receptor interactions, defined alarmin-stromal experiments and ligament-derived extracellular-vesicle transfer are evaluated within their specific experimental contexts, whereas anti-CD74 antibodies, circulating microRNAs, DN2 B-cell changes and the FOXO1-SIRT1 axis remain associative or exploratory. Inhibitors targeting TNF, IL-17A/IL-17F and Janus kinase pathways are clinically effective in defined axSpA populations, whereas IL-23-pathway inhibition has not demonstrated efficacy in established axial disease. Several explanations remain possible, but these trials do not identify a specific IL-23-independent cellular circuit. By considering supportive, conflicting and negative findings together, this review identifies the evidence still needed before candidate mechanisms or biomarkers can inform treatment decisions or help predict structural progression.

items.title: Sustained delivery of TNF-α inhibitors using HAP/PDA-functionalized porous PLGA-based microspheres for rheumatoid arthritis therapy.
items.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitors (TNFi) are a cornerstone of biological therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), yet their clinical efficacy is often compromised by rapid systemic clearance and frequent administration, while preservation of protein bioactivity remains a major challenge for long-acting delivery systems. Here, we report HAP/PDA-functionalized porous poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA)-based microspheres for sustained delivery of TNFi. By integrating hydroxyapatite (HAP)-mediated buffering of the degradation microenvironment with polydopamine (PDA)-enabled interfacial regulation, the composite microspheres enable high protein loading, reduced burst release, and sustained delivery of biologically active TNFi. HAP mitigates degradation-associated acidification, whereas PDA enhances protein retention and regulates release through interfacial interactions. In vitro, TNFi released from the functionalized microspheres retained anti-inflammatory activity, suppressing TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β secretion by M1-polarized macrophages and attenuating inflammation-induced proliferation and migration of rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes. In a collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) rat model, the TNFi-loaded microspheres prolonged apparent systemic TNFi exposure following subcutaneous administration, reduced arthritis severity and joint swelling, and protected against synovial inflammation and cartilage destruction compared with free TNFi, without overt histopathological abnormalities in major organs. These findings support HAP/PDA-functionalized porous PLGA-based microspheres as a long-acting subcutaneous TNFi formulation and illustrate the value of jointly regulating the PLGA degradation microenvironment and the protein-carrier interface.

items.title: Harmonising difficult-to-manage and complex-to-manage psoriatic arthritis: from divergent prevalence estimates to reproducible, mechanism-aware phenotypes.
items.abstract: Difficult-to-manage or complex-to-manage psoriatic arthritis is increasingly recognised in clinical practice, but prevalence estimates remain difficult to interpret because studies differ in denominators, definitions of treatment failure, and methods for distinguishing persistent symptoms from objective inflammation. Building on the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology difficult-to-manage definition and the Group for Research and Assessment of Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis complex-to-manage definition, this Viewpoint proposes an implementation framework to improve reproducibility across registries, trials, and translational studies. We recommend dual-denominator reporting, with estimates presented both in all patients with psoriatic arthritis and in patients exposed to biological or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. We also propose an auditable treatment ledger documenting drug mechanism and class, adequacy of exposure, optimisation attempts, and reasons for discontinuation. After treatment-pathway difficulty is established, patients should be stratified by dominant drivers of persistent burden: inflammatory, non-inflammatory, or mixed. Domain-specific description, impact profiling, disease duration, and prespecified sensitivity analyses should improve comparability and interpretation.

items.title: Pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of early lupus nephritis via a 68 Ga-labeled single-stranded DNA probe.
items.abstract: As a major cause of morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the prognosis of lupus nephritis (LN) critically depends on early detection and timely intervention. However, current diagnostic approaches remain suboptimal: renal biopsy is invasive and unsuitable for longitudinal monitoring, while conventional urine tests lack sensitivity for early-stage disease. Here, we report a molecular imaging strategy designed to target the pathogenic DNA-anti-dsDNA antibody axis for non-invasive detection of LN. We engineered a gallium-68-labeled single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) probe ([ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-ssDNA) and evaluated its diagnostic performance and biosafety in the spontaneous MRL/lpr lupus mouse model. The probe showed disease-associated and sustained renal accumulation in 16-week-old diseased MRL/lpr mice, with progressively increasing kidney-to-background contrast. More importantly, [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-ssDNA enabled detection of renal immune complex deposition as early as 10 weeks of age, preceding abnormalities in conventional renal function markers and positive findings in renal histology by approximately two weeks. Mechanistically, the ssDNA backbone demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, without exacerbating autoimmune phenotypes or inducing Toll-like receptor-mediated signaling pathways. In conclusion, this study establishes a robust proof-of-concept for pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of immune complex deposition. By directly visualizing the disease-driving renal autoantibody deposition at the preclinical stage, prior to overt organ damage, this strategy shifts LN diagnosis to non-invasive, mechanism-based molecular visualization.

items.title: Association between arthritis and asthma: An observational analysis of NHANES and a Mendelian randomization study.
items.abstract: Observational studies have linked arthritis and asthma, but establishing causality is challenging due to confounding. We analyzed 30,001 adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2003-2018) using survey-weighted logistic regression to assess observational associations. To infer causality, we conducted a two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis using publicly available genetic data. In the observational analysis, arthritis was significantly associated with a higher risk of asthma (adjusted odds ratio = 1.96, 95% confidence interval = 1.75-2.19), with similar findings for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA). Mendelian randomization analysis provided evidence for a positive causal effect of genetic predisposition to RA on asthma (inverse-variance weighted odds ratio = 1.037, 95% confidence interval = 1.007-1.068), but found no significant causal effect for OA. This study provides dual evidence supporting a significant and potentially causal relationship between RA and asthma. In contrast, the association with OA appears to be noncausal, likely driven by confounding factors.

items.title: Interleukin-33 as a potential indicator of disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis: a case-control study.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by persistent inflammation and progressive joint damage. Interleukin-33 (IL-33) has been proposed as an indicator of disease activity; however, its clinical relevance remains controversial, as studies report both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects. This case-control study included 44 patients with RA and 44 age- and sex-matched healthy controls recruited from Minia University Hospital, Egypt. Serum IL-33 levels, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), rheumatoid factor (RF) and Disease Activity Score - 28-ESR (DAS28- ESR) were obtained. Medications, specifically disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), were recorded. Associations between IL-33 levels and clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated. Multivariate regression analysis and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed. Serum IL-33 levels were significantly elevated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, with a median of 145 (interquartile range 41.75-193.75), compared to 7 (4.25-11.0) in controls (p < 0.001). IL-33 demonstrated a strong positive correlation with DAS28 scores (Spearman's ρ = 0.935, p < 0.001), as well as with C-reactive protein (p < 0.001) and rheumatoid factor status (p = 0.002). In multivariate regression analysis, IL-33 remained an independent indicator of DAS28 after adjusting for age, sex, CRP and RF. It was identified as a significant predictor (β = 0.838, p < 0.001), accounting for 83% of the variance in disease activity (adjusted R 2  = 0.83). ROC curve analysis also showed good discrimination for high disease activity (n = 8)(AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.807-0.986). At the selected IL-33 cut-off of 300 pg/mL, sensitivity was 66.7% and specificity was 100%. Serum IL-33 levels are strongly associated with disease activity in RA and may be an indicator of inflammatory burden.

items.title: Serologic Discrimination of Histologic Classes in Lupus Nephritis: A Cross-Sectional Analysis with Exploratory 12-Month Outcomes.
items.abstract: Anti-dsDNA positivity and hypocomplementemia are markers of active lupus nephritis (LN), but their ability to discriminate between histologic phenotypes remains underexplored, particularly for mixed proliferative/membranous LN (mixed LN). We compared baseline serologic markers across proliferative LN, membranous LN, and mixed LN, and evaluated their discriminative performance for histologic class. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study of 132 patients with biopsy-proven LN, categorized according to the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classification into proliferative LN (class III/IV), membranous LN (class V), and mixed LN (class III/IV+V). Baseline anti-dsDNA and complements C3 and C4 were compared across groups. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed the ability of individual and combined markers to discriminate between histologic classes. Kidney outcomes at 12 months were explored in a secondary cohort (n=88). Of 132 patients, 57 had proliferative LN, 32 had membranous LN, and 43 had mixed LN. Anti-dsDNA was significantly higher, and C3 and C4 significantly lower, in proliferative and mixed LN compared to membranous LN (P<0.05 for all), while proliferative and mixed LN did not differ significantly. On ROC analysis, individual markers achieved AUCs of 0.68-0.71 for distinguishing proliferative or mixed LN from membranous LN, with combined models yielding AUCs of 0.73. However, discrimination between proliferative and mixed LN was poor (combined AUC 0.62). At 12 months, kidney outcomes were comparable across groups. Mixed LN exhibits a serologic profile resembling proliferative LN, both sharing elevated anti-dsDNA and low complement levels, but distinct from membranous LN. Serology could inform suspicion for LN class but cannot replace kidney biopsy.

items.title: Glucocorticoid purchases and methotrexate persistence in early rheumatoid arthritis in Finland.
items.abstract: This study aimed to explore purchases of methotrexate (MTX), biological disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs), Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis), and glucocorticoids (GCs) in early rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in Finland. The study included 3046 monitored patients with early RA, who obtained reimbursement for RA medication during 2016-2020. The patients were divided into three groups according to the number of GC tablet purchases during 6 months after the reimbursement day: Group 0, no GC purchases; Group 1, purchased < 90 tablets; Group 2, purchased ≥ 90 tablets. Medication purchases were tracked in 6 month periods until the end of 2021. Of the monitored early RA patients, 68% purchased GCs during the initial 6 months and 43% during 6-11 months after the reimbursement date. Over 90% of the patients purchased MTX during the first year in all groups. Patients in Group 2 had the highest baseline disease activity. After the first year, the percentage of bDMARD purchasers (11% vs 6.8%, p = 0.03) and MTX users (79% vs 74%, p = 0.06) was higher in Group 2 than in Group 0. Nevertheless, persistence with analysed anti-rheumatic medications remained similar, with no statistically significant differences, during the whole follow-up period in all groups. In early RA, the use of oral GCs is common and continues longer than recommended by the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR). Persistence with treatment with MTX, bDMARDs, and JAKis in patients who continued medication was not influenced by the initial GC regimen.

items.title: Janus Kinase inhibitors in refractory Takayasu arteritis: a systematic review and proportion meta-analysis of efficacy and safety.
items.abstract: Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a rare chronic granulomatous vasculitis affecting large arteries, causing recurrent disease despite standard treatment. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate efficacy and safety of Janus kinase inhibitors in patients with refractory Takayasu arteritis. We searched five major databases from inception through July 16, 2026, for observational cohorts, non-randomized interventional studies, and case series including ≥5 patients. Eligible studies enrolled adults with refractory TAK treated with JAK inhibitors. Data were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane ROBINS-I and Joanna Briggs Institute tools. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261469541). GRADE was used to assess certainty of primary efficacy outcomes. Eleven studies comprising 185 patients were included. The pooled clinical remission rate was 64% (95% CI, 55%-72%; I²=0%), while complete and partial remission rates were 65% (95% CI, 55%-74%) and 8% (95% CI, 4%-17%), respectively. Pooled rates of no response and relapse were 24% and 14%, respectively. Imaging improvement or stabilization was observed in 44% of patients, while glucocorticoid-sparing effects occurred in 56%. Adverse events occurred in 10% of patients, and 7% discontinued treatment because of adverse events. GRADE certainty was very low for all assessed outcomes. JAK inhibitors demonstrate promising clinical efficacy and a potentially manageable safety profile in refractory TAK. However, the available evidence is predominantly observational and therefore subject to confounding and other sources of bias. High-quality prospective and randomized studies are needed to establish their efficacy, comparative effectiveness, and long-term safety.

items.title: Long-term efficacy and safety of upadacitinib in patients with polyarticular-course juvenile idiopathic arthritis: 48 week results from the SELECT-YOUTH open-label study.
items.abstract: The phase 1 SELECT-YOUTH trial demonstrated efficacy and safety of upadacitinib for pcJIA in pediatric patients. This second interim analysis incorporates the results from an additional cohort providing efficacy results up to 48 weeks and cumulative safety up to 156 weeks. 122 patients with pcJIA, aged 2 to < 18 years received upadacitinib, dosed either twice-daily oral solution or once-daily extended-release tablet, based on body weight. Analyses included patients who received at least one dose. Efficacy and safety outcomes were evaluated through week 156 using as observed and non-responder imputation methods. Efficacy was reported up to 48 weeks; safety was assessed at all study time points. Efficacy included JIA-ACR 30/50/70/90/100 response rates, Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score (JADAS)-27, C-HAQ, and pain. At 48 weeks, JIA-ACR response rates were: 96.3% (JIA-ACR30), 93.6% (JIA-ACR50), 89.0% (JIA-ACR70), 72.5% (JIA-ACR90), 57.8% (JIA-ACR100). Low disease activity (JADAS-27 [CRP] ≤ 3.8) was achieved by 79.4%, with 49.5% reaching inactive disease status (JADAS-27 [CRP] ≤ 1). C-HAQ change from baseline to week 48 was -0.64 (n = 108) and rapid improvement in pain was evident by week 12 and persisted throughout 48 weeks. Treatment-emergent adverse events were generally mild to moderate, occurring at 499.6 events per 100 patient-years (E/100 PY; n = 122). Most frequent events (per 100 PY) of special interest were hepatic disorders (7.5), bone fractures (4.3), and CPK elevation (3.5). No deaths occurred. In the SELECT-YOUTH trial, bodyweight-based dosing of upadacitinib maintained efficacy in pediatric patients with pcJIA, and its safety profile was consistent with established safety profile. items.title: Herpes zoster in rheumatoid arthritis and in relation to biologic/targeted synthetic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs: a Swedish national study.
items.abstract: To assess and compare the incidences of herpes zoster (HZ) in rheumatoid arthritis patients (RA) receiving biologic/targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (b/tsDMARDs), in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA, and general population. We identified all patients with RA in Sweden 2014-2024, and b/tsDMARD starts among them, through register linkages. For each b/ts-DMARD treatment start, five age/sex-matched population controls were selected. A history of HZ was defined as a listing with an ICD-10 code for HZ and/or dispensation of an antiviral drug up to one year before treatment start. Incident HZ was defined as the first HZ ICD-10 code during follow-up accompanied by prescription of an antiviral within 90 days. 77694 unique RA patients contributed to the following: 69962 subjects in the b/tsDMARD-naïve cohort, and 20033 TNFi-, 9410 non-TNFi-, and 4023 JAKi-treatment episodes. Based on 95 incident HZ cases (incidence rate (IR) 2.0, 95% confidence interval 1.6-2.4 per1000 person-years) with TNFi, 55 cases (IR 2.4, 95% CI 1.8-3.1) with non-TNFi, 41 cases (IR 5.1, 95% CI 3.7-6.9) with JAKi, 561 cases (IR 1.5, 95% CI 1.4-1.6) in b/tsDMARD-naive RA and 494 cases (IR 0.6, 95% CI 0.6-0.7) in the general population, the multivariable-adjusted hazard ratio (using TNFi as reference) with JAKi was HR = 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-3.0 and HR = 0.9; 95% CI 0.6-1.3 for non-TNFi. The incidence of a first ever HZ is higher in b/tsDMARD-naïve patients compared to general population, is further and similarly increased in patients receiving TNFi or non-TNFi, and yet higher in those starting JAKi.

items.title: Comparison of JAK inhibitors and biologics with respect to pain reduction in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: data from the KOBIO registry.
items.abstract: To compare the pain-reducing efficacy of Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis) and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Patients with RA enrolled in the Korean College of Rheumatology Biologics and Targeted Therapy (KOBIO) registry were grouped according to use of JAKis, TNFis, and non-TNFi bDMARDs. The primary outcome was to compare the changes in pain on a numeric rating scale (NRS, range 0-10) between enrolment and first follow-up. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify the factors associated with a low pain NRS score (< 2) and retention at the 1-year follow-up. The analysis included 2,415 patients with RA in the JAKis (n = 422), TNFis (n = 1,148), and non-TNFi bDMARDs groups (n = 845). The change in pain NRS was significantly greater in the JAKis group than in the TNFis group (2.8 ± 2.5 vs. 2.3 ± 2.9, respectively; p < 0.01). The adjusted mean additional pain reduction was significantly greater in the JAKis than in the TNFis group (-0.42, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.73 to -0.10). The adjusted odds ratio (OR) for achieving a pain NRS score < 2 with initial drug retention at 1 year follow-up was significantly lower in the TNFis (OR = 0.515; 95% CI: 0.406-0.652) and non-TNFi bDMARDs (OR = 0.586; 95% CI: 0.458-0.751) groups than in the JAKis group. Among patients who achieved treatment response and remained on therapy, JAKis were associated with greater improvement in pain control than TNFis.

items.title: Comprehensive Analysis Identifies FCER1A as a Potential Link Between Immune Dysregulation and Therapeutic Responses in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Gastric Cancer.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients exhibit an elevated risk of gastric cancer (GC), yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. This study presents a novel integrative bioinformatics framework to identify shared molecular signatures between SLE and GC and to assess their prognostic implications. This study retrieved microarray data from the GSE50772 and GSE81622 datasets in the GEO database and RNA-seq data from the GC cohort in TCGA. Following screening, this study identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and further characterized them based on their differential expression. This study identified the common DEGs (co-DEGs) and performed GO and KEGG pathway analyses to identify relevant pathways, immune infiltration, and gene diagnostic value in the context of SLE and GC. By analyzing three independent datasets (GSE50772, GSE81622, and TCGA_STAD), this study identified 12 co-DEGs, among which FCER1A was validated as an independent prognostic factor for GC through multivariate Cox regression (HR = 1.184, P = 0.026). In addition, FCER1A expression showed significant positive correlations with infiltration of multiple immune cell types, including macrophages (P = 3.38e-27, r = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.44-0.59), CD4+ T cells (P = 7.32e-18, r = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.34-0.51), and neutrophils (P = 5.82e-12, r = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.25-0.43), suggesting its role in shaping the tumor immune microenvironment. Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed that high FCER1A expression predicted poorer overall survival (P = 0.036) and first progression (P = 0.029). In this study, FCER1A was identified as the key gene affected by the combination of SLE and GC. This study is the first to systematically link FCER1A-mediated immune infiltration to prognosis in SLE-associated GC, offering a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this understudied comorbidity.

items.title: C5a receptor inhibition and minimal steroids for induction of remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis.
items.abstract: C5a receptor (C5aR) inhibition with avacopan has enabled cumulative glucocorticoid (GC) dose reduction in ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV); however, real-world steroid use remains high. This study evaluates a minimal-GC plus avacopan-based regimen against standard-of-care GC for clinical efficacy, renal recovery, urinary biomarkers, and patient-reported outcomes (AAV-PRO). We hypothesised that this regimen would permit substantial GC reduction while maintaining clinical disease control and renal recovery. This two-centre retrospective study included 126 patients with newly diagnosed or relapsing AAV (70 avacopan; 56 GC). The avacopan group followed the minimal-GC plus avacopan-based regimen: prednisolone 30 mg daily for one week, then 20 mg for one week, with no protocolised upfront intravenous methylprednisolone; the GC group received a standard high-dose oral GC taper (from 1 mg/kg, capped at 60 mg/day). Both received standard induction with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Outcomes included 12-month sustained remission, eGFR change, safety, AAV-PRO scores, and urinary sCD163, MCP-1 and C5a trajectories. Baseline characteristics were comparable, with median presenting eGFR 23 versus 25 mL/min/1.73 m² (P = 0.31). Median 12-month cumulative prednisolone was 390 mg with avacopan versus 3535 mg with GC (P < 0.001). Observed sustained remission was 93% versus 91% (P = 0.75) and relapse 6% versus 11% (P = 0.30). Median eGFR increase was 20 versus 18 mL/min/1.73 m² (P = 0.32), with no significant difference among those presenting with eGFR < 15 (P = 0.20). Severe infection rates did not differ significantly (6% versus 9%). AAV-PRO scores were significantly lower with avacopan (median 97 versus 197; P = 0.04). No significant between-group difference in biomarker trajectories was detected. In this observational cohort, the minimal-GC plus avacopan-based regimen showed no statistically significant differences in clinical or renal outcomes versus high-dose steroids while reducing cumulative GC exposure by ∼90%. These real-world observations support the feasibility of substantial upfront GC minimisation but should be regarded as supportive rather than confirmatory.

items.title: Non-Invasive Myocardial Work Assessment of Subclinical Left Ventricular Dysfunction in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
items.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease associated with increased cardiovascular risk. This study aimed to evaluate subclinical left ventricular (LV) dysfunction in patients with AS using non-invasive myocardial work analysis. 50 patients with AS and 44 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Comprehensive clinical characteristics were documented for all participants. Two dimensional dynamic images of the apical four-chamber, two chamber, and three-chamber views were collected from all subjects, with three consecutive cardiac cycles recorded for each view. LV myocardial strain parameters, including global longitudinal strain (GLS) and peak strain dispersion (PSD), as well as myocardial work indices, including global work index (GWI), and global constructive work (GCW), global wasted work (GWW), global work efficiency (GWE), were obtained and subsequently analyzed. Compared with controls, patients with AS had lower absolute GLS (18.46±2.00% vs.19.41±1.91%, p = 0.021), higher PSD ( 47 . 20 ± 13 . 25 vs . 39 . 32 ± 9 . 10 ms , p = 0 . 001 ) and GWW ([106.00 (68.75-140.00) vs. 61.00 (49.25-81.25) mmHg%, P < 0.001), along with lower GWI(1679.26±226.70 vs. 1780.84±209.25 mmHg%, P < 0.05) and GWE (94.08±2.68% vs. 96.32±0.93%, P < 0.001). Furthermore, PSD was positively correlated with GWW (r = 0.59, P < 0.001) and negatively correlated with GWE (r = -0.65, P < 0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, LV mass index, and GLS, AS remained associated with higher PSD ( p = 0 . 007 ) , higher GWW ( P < 0 . 001 ) , and lower GWE (P < 0.001), whereas the associations with GWI and GCW were not statistically significant. Patients with AS exhibited increased LV mechanical dispersion and wasted myocardial work and reduced myocardial work efficiency. These alterations persisted after adjustment for GLS, suggesting that PSD and myocardial work analysis may provide complementary information for characterizing subclinical LV dysfunction in AS.

items.title: N6-methyladenosine epitranscriptomic alterations and their potential implications for maternal-fetal immune tolerance in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome.
items.abstract: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome (OAPS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by the persistent presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL), such as anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, in women experiencing obstetric complications. While vascular thrombotic events were considered the primary pathogenic mechanism in recent years, evidence indicates that the maternal-fetal interface in OAPS is altered by other underlying pathways, such as direct impairment of trophoblast invasion, dysregulation of immune cell activation, and platelet complement activation. These pathways act synergistically to compromise the immunological tolerance essential for fetal development. In parallel, recent research has highlighted the role of epigenetic modifications that maintain placental homeostasis and trophoblast proliferation. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant messenger RNA (mRNA) modification in mammals and plays a fundamental role in the maternal-fetal interface and the generation of immune tolerance. Specifically, the upregulation of m6A-modulating proteins is associated with recurrent pregnancy loss, defective placental artery remodeling, and HLA-G expression, a key factor in fetomaternal tolerance. Despite this knowledge, to date, no review has integrated m6A modification as a key mediator in the loss of immune tolerance in the context of adverse obstetric outcomes, including fetal growth restriction (FGR). In this review, we proposing a hypothetical model in which aPL exposure could induce alterations in the m6A methylation pattern that may affect the HLA-G/regulatory T cells (Treg)/uterine NK cells (uNK) axis potentially contributing to fetal loss, operating independently or in conjunction with prothrombotic mechanisms.

items.title: Prevalence of depression in childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (cSLE) is frequently associated with psychological symptoms, particularly depression. However, there remains a lack of quantitative evidence regarding the prevalence of screening-positive depressive symptoms based on the currently available evidence. In this context, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis addressing this important issue. Three medical databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library were utilized in this study. We included studies that reported on cSLE patients experiencing depression for a meta-analysis, without publication language restrictions. Anxiety were included as secondary outcomes. STATA software were employed to synthesize the results as well as to assess heterogeneity and publication bias. Totally 12 eligible studies encompassing 652 patients were incorporated into this meta-analysis. Each of the publications included exhibited commendable methodological rigor, with Newcastle-Ottawa scores no less than 6. The pooled prevalence was [32.6%] (95% CI: [24.5%-41.8%]). Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I 2  = [73.66%]; τ 2  = [0.26] on the logit scale). Subsequent subgroup analysis indicated that the prevalence of depression varied according to the different screening tools used: it was found to be 26% with CDI (95% CI: 0.18-0.34, P  = 0.023, I 2  = 61.8%), 41% with PHQ-9 (95% CI: 0.20-0.63, P  < 0.001, I 2  = 90.7%), and 37% with other tools such as BSI, BDI, and CES-D (95% CI: 0.21-0.53, P  = 0.031, I 2  = 71.3%). Furthermore, the Egger's test indicates that publication bias is insignificant among the studies included. For secondary outcome, pooled results indicated that the prevalence of anxiety among cSLE patients was 29.0% (95% CI: 0.19-0.42, P  < 0.001), exhibiting relatively high heterogeneity (I 2  = 61.8%, τ 2  = [0.13] on the logit scale). Approximately one-third of patients with cSLE screened positive for depressive symptoms, underscoring the critical need for routine mental health screening in clinical care. These prevalence estimates should be interpreted with caution due to methodological and clinical heterogeneity across studies and do not reflect the prevalence of clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder.

items.title: Just One Move: co-design and usability testing of a digital physical activity behavior change platform for people with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) affects 18 million people worldwide, leading to debilitating symptoms and increased cardiovascular disease risk. Regular physical activity can address these challenges, yet people with RA face barriers to physical activity and lack tailored support. Digital interventions offer a resource-efficient strategy for increasing physical activity. To improve their effectiveness and implementation, stronger end-user engagement and behavioral science integration is needed. Alongside physical activity experts, rheumatology providers, and people with RA, we completed preparatory research to inform the co-design of an RA-specific digital physical activity intervention: JustOneMove.ca. The present study presents learnings from the co-design process, outlines the resultant intervention, and summarizes usability survey findings. The study leveraged patient-oriented research, user-centered design, and behavioral science frameworks (behavior change wheel, theoretical domains framework). After mapping physical activity barriers to these frameworks, Just One Move was co-designed via a 4-step user-centered process (Phase 1). We collaborated with people with RA and web design experts to review, design, refine, and develop the intervention using design sprint methodology. Data on resources required and partner involvement during Phase 1 were summarized descriptively. A mixed methods survey (Phase 2) gathered perspectives on usability and usefulness. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and qualitative content analysis. Co-design was completed in 7 months by a team of 20 people with RA, 5 researchers (rheumatology, physiotherapy, behavioral science), and 2 experts in healthcare design and web development. Co-design blended research evidence and user preferences through design thinking. Challenges included balancing creativity with feasibility and defining clear expectations. The Just One Move intervention includes: a library of RA-friendly movements, a guided action planner, a collection of inspiring stories from people with RA, and an expert toolkit with tips for moving well with RA. Across 37 users (median age: 62.0), average usability was 4.0/5 and usefulness was 3.7/5. Just One Move was easy to use and inspired confidence to move more. However, users requested clearer instructions and more customizable content. Evidence-informed co-design can produce high-quality digital physical activity interventions for people with RA. Future work will examine the effectiveness of JustOneMove.ca.

items.title: Programmed cell death in primary Sjögren's disease: regulatory network analysis and therapeutic prospects evaluation.
items.abstract: Primary Sjögren's disease (SjD) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic inflammation of exocrine glands, such as the salivary and lacrimal glands. The pathogenesis of SjD remains largely unclear, and there are currently no effective curative therapies. Programmed cell death (PCD) and its regulatory network play a crucial role in the onset and progression of SjD. PCD mechanisms such as apoptosis, autophagy, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis are widely involved in the pathological mechanisms and prognosis of SjD by regulating the immune-inflammatory microenvironment, mediating the imbalance of glandular epithelial cell homeostasis, and affecting the release and clearance of self-antigens. Based on this, targeting the regulation of PCD to treat SjD has become a new therapeutic strategy. Existing evidence indicates that modulating the expression of certain miRNAs and proteins, as well as employing modern medical drugs, traditional Chinese medicine, and their active components, can influence the pathological processes of glandular inflammation and tissue damage in SjD through the regulation of apoptosis, autophagy, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis. These findings provide potential targets for precise treatment based on the PCD network.This article reviews recent relevant literature to clarify the relationship between PCD and SjD, and focuses on the molecular regulatory networks of different types of PCD in SjD and their therapeutic prospects, aiming to provide new ideas and insights for the prevention and treatment of SjD.

items.title: Case Report: KBG syndrome in an adult presenting with diabetes, gout, and hypogonadism.
items.abstract: KBG syndrome (MIM #148050) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ANKRD11 or 16q24.3 microdeletions, classically recognized in children through macrodontia, short stature, skeletal anomalies, and neurodevelopmental delay. How the syndrome presents to adult internal medicine remains poorly documented. A 31-year-old man was admitted with new-onset diabetes (blood glucose 20.0 mmol/L) and an acute gout flare, superimposed on congenital sensorineural deafness, repaired cryptorchidism, and 10 years of recurrent gout. Examination revealed macrodontia of the upper central incisors, kyphoscoliosis, brachydactyly with fifth-finger clinodactyly, bilateral gynecomastia, and small soft testes. Investigations showed preserved β-cell reserve with delayed insulin and C-peptide peaks, negative islet autoantibodies, repeatedly borderline-low testosterone with inadequately normal gonadotropins, and 24-h urinary uric acid excretion at the lower end of the reference range. Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness was initially suspected because diabetes coexisted with deafness, but the burden of congenital anomalies prompted trio whole-exome sequencing, which identified a de novo heterozygous ANKRD11 frameshift (NM_013275.6: c.1903_1907del, p.Lys635Glnfs*26). He was treated with liraglutide, febuxostat, colchicine, and atorvastatin. Over 33 months of follow-up, glycated hemoglobin remained between 4.5% and 5.3% and thyroid function normalized, yet serum urate stayed markedly elevated at nearly every routine measurement, and one gout flare required readmission. This case illustrates delayed recognition of KBG syndrome during adulthood: the characteristic dental, skeletal, and developmental signs had been present since early childhood, yet the syndrome was named only when an acquired metabolic cluster-diabetes, gout, and hypogonadism-brought him to adult endocrine care. The decade of gout preceding glucose intolerance is, to our knowledge, the first such report in KBG syndrome and remains a single observation; whether it reflects an intrinsic urate-handling defect is a hypothesis that merits further study rather than an established association. Careful attention to dental, skeletal, and developmental clues in atypical diabetes can end a long diagnostic odyssey.

items.title: Sjögren's disease complicated by TAFRO syndrome: a case report of fever and lymphadenopathy with literature review.
items.abstract: TAFRO syndrome, a fulminant subtype of idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD), is characterized by thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly. Its occurrence in patients with pre-existing Sjögren's disease (SjD) is rare and poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. A 59-year-old male with a 10-year history of SjD complicated by primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) presented with a 3-month history of recurrent epistaxis, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings revealed severe thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and positive anti-SSA/Ro and AMA-M2 antibodies. PET-CT demonstrated generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and bilateral pleural effusions. An extensive workup excluded infection, lymphoma, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Excisional lymph node biopsy confirmed Castleman disease (plasmacytic type), and integration of clinical and pathological findings established the diagnosis of TAFRO syndrome. The patient failed to respond to high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and dexamethasone combined with ruxolitinib. Definitive disease control was ultimately achieved with the RPAD chemotherapy regimen (rituximab, bortezomib, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone), leading to sustained clinical remission with normalized platelet count at 12-month follow-up. This case highlights that TAFRO syndrome can arise on the background of chronic autoimmune disease as a life-threatening cytokine storm, and may be mistaken for refractory HLH. Early recognition through systematic exclusion of mimics and histological confirmation is essential. In patients who fail conventional and cytokine-directed therapies, intensive multi-agent chemotherapy such as the RPAD regimen may be an effective salvage option.

items.title: The role of 18 F-FDG PET-CT in predicting progressive pulmonary fibrosis in idiopathic inflammatory myopathy associated interstitial lung disease.
items.abstract: This study aims to investigate the role of 18 F-FDG PET-CT in the development of progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy-associated interstitial lung disease (IIM-ILD) and to develop a predictive nomogram model. This study retrospectively included patients diagnosed with IIM-ILD who underwent 18 F-FDG PET-CT at Ruijin Hospital between 2018 and 2024. The baseline characteristics, IIM types, myositis antibodies, laboratory tests, pulmonary function, ILD subtypes, 18 F-FDG PET-CT findings, and treatment were collected. Enrolled patients were divided into PPF and non-PPF groups according to diagnostic criteria. Clinical features were compared between the two groups, and logistic regression analysis was performed to identify risk factors for PPF. All identified risk factors were combined to construct the predictive nomogram. Receiver operating characteristic curve, calibration plot, and decision curve analysis were used to evaluate the accuracy and efficiency of this predictive model. Additionally, we drew the survival curve of PPF and non-PPF, and compared the maximum standardized uptake value (SUV max ) between short-term death and long-term survival. A total of 71 eligible IIM-ILD patients were included, of whom 29 developed PPF within one year of follow-up. Multivariate analysis revealed that bilateral lung SUV max and FVC%pred were associated with the occurrence of PPF. The calibration plot demonstrated excellent agreement between the predicted and actual observed probability of PPF (Hosmer-Lemeshow test: P = 0.143). The predictive nomogram achieved an area under the curve of 0.887 (95% CI : 0.805-0.969). The SUV max in the lungs was significantly higher in the PPF group than in the non-PPF group ( P  < 0.001). Moreover, lung SUVmax was significantly higher in patients who died within one year than in those who survived for more than five years ( P  = 0.014). In addition, patients with PPF had a significantly lower survival rate than those without PPF ( P  = 0.040). 18 F-FDG PET-CT and FVC% pred are associated with the occurrence of PPF. The prognosis of PPF is poor, and high SUV max is correlated with short-term mortality. Exhibiting robust discrimination and calibration, this nomogram holds potential for clinical application.

items.title: Glucocorticoid dose at 26 weeks and subsequent relapse in anti-ARS antibody-positive antisynthetase syndrome under concomitant immunosuppressive therapy: a retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) remain central to antisynthetase syndrome (ASSD) treatment, but relapse during tapering and GC-related adverse effects remain important concerns. Because GC-related morbidity may emerge early, minimizing GC exposure while maintaining disease control is important. Whether the GC dose during early tapering is associated with subsequent relapse remains unclear. We investigated whether a GC dose of ≤5 mg/day at approximately 6 months was associated with subsequent relapse in anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (ARS) antibody-positive ASSD receiving concomitant immunosuppressive therapy. We retrospectively analyzed 45 patients with anti-ARS antibody-positive ASSD treated with systemic GCs and concomitant immunosuppressive therapy. We performed a week-26 landmark analysis, representing approximately 6 months after treatment initiation, among patients who remained relapse-free and under observation through the landmark. Subsequent relapse-free survival was compared between patients receiving GC ≤5 and >5 mg/day in prednisolone equivalents at the landmark. During overall follow-up, 26 of 45 patients (58%) experienced relapse, whereas only 4 (8.9%) relapsed before week 26. Among 41 patients who remained relapse-free and under observation through the landmark, 17 were receiving GC ≤5 mg/day and 24 were receiving >5 mg/day. During post-landmark follow-up, 22 patients experienced subsequent relapse. Patients receiving GC ≤5 mg/day at week 26 had higher subsequent relapse-free survival than those receiving >5 mg/day (log-rank p  = 0.007). In multivariable analyses, GC ≤5 mg/day at week 26 was associated with a lower risk of subsequent relapse after adjustment for Raynaud phenomenon and initial GC dose (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.08-0.86; p  = 0.027) and after adjustment for Raynaud phenomenon and anti-Jo-1 positivity (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10-0.99; p  = 0.047). Among patients with anti-ARS antibody-positive ASSD receiving concomitant immunosuppressive therapy who remained relapse-free and under observation through the week-26 landmark, a GC dose ≤5 mg/day was associated with a lower risk of subsequent relapse. Although these findings should not be generalized to all patients or interpreted as establishing an optimal tapering target, the GC dose at this landmark may serve as a clinically useful marker of early disease control or treatment response. Prospective studies are warranted to validate its clinical significance.

items.title: An LRRC37A2 single nucleotide variant is associated with emphysema in Japanese patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Extra-articular manifestations commonly complicate RA and include chronic lung diseases (CLDs), e.g. interstitial lung disease or emphysema (EMP). These confer a poor prognosis. Genetic studies of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or EMP were conducted. However, there are limited genetic studies on EMP in RA. We examined whether a single nucleotide variant associated with susceptibility to IPF was associated with EMP in Japanese RA patients. rs199526 [C/G] genotyping of LRRC37A2 in samples from 88 RA patients with EMP and 425 RA lacking CLD was conducted. LRRC37A2 rs199526C was significantly associated to EMP in RA according to an allele model [ P  = 0.0083, odds ratio (OR) 1.72 (95% CI 1.14, 2.59)] or a recessive model for major alleles [ P  = 0.0139, OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.13, 2.94)], although it was protectively associated against IPF in European populations. Multiple logistic regression analyses revealed an independent association with age, Steinbrocker stage and Steinbrocker class. An association between LRRC37A2 rs199526 and RA per se was detected. An association between rs199526 and EMP was noted in Japanese RA patients. Differential roles of the single nucleotide variant between EMP in RA and IPF were suggested.

items.title: Gastric Pancreatic Heterotopia and Bronchoesophageal Fistula in a Patient With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Antiphospholipid Syndrome: A Case Report.
items.abstract: A 23-year-old woman with documented systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and a recent pulmonary embolism requiring anticoagulation presented with acute hematemesis. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a small mid-esophageal opening with mucus and air passage and an ulcerated gastric subepithelial lesion, without an identifiable active bleeding source. Chest computed tomography with oral contrast demonstrated a left bronchoesophageal fistula (BEF). Endoscopic ultrasonography showed a 20.8 × 15.4 mm hypoechoic lesion arising from the fourth sonographic layer of the gastric wall, corresponding to the muscularis propria, in the fundus/body region. The lesion was ulcerated and endophytic, raising suspicion for a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). EUS-guided tissue acquisition was deferred because of anticoagulation, and laparoscopic resection was performed. Histopathological examination revealed Heinrich type I gastric pancreatic heterotopia (GPH) involving the submucosa and muscularis propria, with pancreatic acini, ducts, and islet cells, accompanied by focal pancreatitis and chronic active gastritis. No malignancy was identified, and the surgical margins were free. Perioperative anticoagulation was managed by temporary interruption of warfarin with therapeutic enoxaparin bridging. The available records did not document definitive fistula-directed treatment or establish whether the BEF subsequently resolved or persisted. Although GPH and BEF coexisted in this patient, no direct anatomical or causal relationship could be established, and the source of hematemesis remained undetermined. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of concurrent gastric and esophageal abnormalities in a patient with competing thrombotic and bleeding risks and underscores the importance of multimodal imaging, histopathological confirmation, and individualized perioperative anticoagulation management.

items.title: Measuring treatment response in psoriatic arthritis: comparison between PSoriatic Arthritis Response Criteria and Disease Activity Score.
items.abstract: Despite current UK guidelines recommending the use of the PSoriatic Arthritis Response Criteria (PsARC) to assess response to advanced targeted therapies in PsA patients, some clinicians use the 28-joint Disease Activity Score (DAS28), primarily developed for RA. Concordance of the two scores in PsA patients commencing advanced therapies has not previously been explored and is investigated here. Utilising data from the Outcomes of Treatment in Psoriatic Arthritis Study Syndicate (OUTPASS - RDN-CPMS 13910) cohort, a UK multicentre, observational study, components of PsARC and DAS28 scores were calculated at baseline (pretreatment), 3 months and 6 months following treatment, where available. DAS28-based good/moderate responses were combined and compared with PsARC responder status and agreement tested using the prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa test. Of 413 patients, 78% were classified as responders by PsARC at 3 months and 73% at 6 months and 80% by DAS28 at both 3 and 6 months. Of 218 visits, where data were recorded for patients with both PsARC and DAS28 at 3 or 6 months, 17.9% were overall discordant. Prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa values revealed 'substantial agreement' (64.22%) between the two scores. Further analysis between the overall concordant/discordant populations showed significant differences with PsARC patient global assessments (PtGAs), ( P  = 0.02). PsARC and DAS28-based response criteria show 'substantial agreement', supporting the use of either score in patients commencing advanced therapies. PsARC PtGA was the sole significantly different ( P  < 0.05) subcomponent between the discordant and concordant groups, highlighting an importance in considering patient perspectives and psychosocial factors affecting response to treatment.

items.title: Early recognition of a macrophage activation-associated hyperinflammatory state in anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease: a case report.
items.abstract: Anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) antibody-positive dermatomyositis is frequently complicated by rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) and is associated with poor prognosis. In some cases, excessive systemic inflammation related to macrophage activation may occur and contribute to disease severity. We report the case of a 59-year-old Japanese woman with anti-MDA5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis complicated by RP-ILD. She initially presented with skin rash and dyspnea, followed by declining vital capacity and progressive proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory evaluation revealed cytopenia and hyperferritinemia. Bone marrow examination performed because of leukopenia demonstrated hemophagocytosis by activated macrophages. Although the diagnostic criteria for macrophage activation syndrome were not fully met, these findings suggested a macrophage activation-associated hyperinflammatory state. In view of the progressive interstitial lung disease and suspected hyperinflammation, therapeutic intensification was undertaken by adding plasma exchange and intravenous cyclophosphamide to corticosteroids and tacrolimus. Following treatment escalation, cytopenia, pulmonary function, and muscle strength gradually improved. This case highlights the importance of recognizing macrophage activation-associated hyperinflammation in anti-MDA5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis. Early recognition and prompt therapeutic intensification may contribute to improved clinical outcomes.

items.title: Hepatic steatosis and its associated factors in patients with rheumatoid arthritis based on quantitative assessment by ultrasound-derived fat fraction.
items.abstract: To investigate the prevalence and associated factors of hepatic steatosis in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and to evaluate the associations of methotrexate (MTX) cumulative exposure, inflammatory burden, and metabolic factors with hepatic steatosis. A total of 118 patients with RA were enrolled in this single-center cross-sectional study. Demographic characteristics, clinical data, laboratory indicators, and medication history were collected. Hepatic fat content was quantitatively assessed using ultrasound-derived fat fraction (UDFF), with hepatic steatosis defined as UDFF ≥ 6%. Clinical characteristics were compared between patients with and without hepatic steatosis. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with hepatic steatosis, and multivariate linear regression was used to analyze factors associated with continuous UDFF levels. An exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate the discriminatory ability of cumulative MTX exposure, and exploratory joint stratification by cumulative MTX exposure and CRP level was conducted using Firth penalized logistic regression. The prevalence of hepatic steatosis was 49.2% (58/118). Compared with patients without hepatic steatosis, patients with hepatic steatosis had significantly higher BMI, AST, ALT, triglycerides, fasting glucose, TyG index, FIB-4 index, and cumulative MTX dose, whereas CRP levels were significantly lower. In the fully adjusted logistic regression model, older age (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.02-1.17, P = 0.014), higher BMI (OR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.32-2.14, P < 0.001), higher TyG index (OR = 3.33, 95% CI: 1.07-12.00, P = 0.047), and higher cumulative MTX dose (per 100 mg: OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.01-1.18, P = 0.034) were positively associated with hepatic steatosis, whereas CRP was negatively associated (per 5 mg/L: OR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.79-0.98, P = 0.023). Multivariate linear regression showed consistent associations of BMI, TyG index, cumulative MTX dose, age, and CRP with continuous UDFF levels. Exploratory ROC analysis showed modest discriminatory ability of cumulative MTX exposure for hepatic steatosis (AUC = 0.698, 95% CI: 0.604-0.793), and identified a cohort-specific cut-off of 456 mg. In exploratory joint stratification, the high MTX (> 456 mg) plus low CRP (≤ 8 mg/L) subgroup showed higher odds of hepatic steatosis compared with the low MTX (≤ 456 mg) plus high CRP (> 8 mg/L) reference group (adjusted OR = 14.70, 95% CI: 3.33-86.40, P < 0.001), although the interaction term was not statistically significant. Hepatic steatosis is common in patients with RA. Metabolic factors, particularly BMI and TyG index, together with cumulative MTX exposure, were associated with hepatic steatosis and higher UDFF levels. The inverse association between CRP and hepatic steatosis may reflect contemporaneous disease-control status or treatment exposure rather than a causal effect. The combination of high cumulative MTX exposure and low CRP may help identify a subgroup warranting further evaluation, but this finding should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

items.title: Challenges in linking interferon signatures to clinical trajectories in juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
items.abstract: Based on the recent finding that higher baseline expression of interferon (IFN)-driven gene signature in blood positively correlates with good response to methotrexate (MTX) in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), this study tested the hypothesis that baseline IFN scores differ significantly between trajectory groups of response to MTX, defined by machine learning models enabling clinicians to predict not just the likelihood, but the specific longitudinal course of therapeutic response. Longitudinal clinical data from 699 children and young people (CYP) with active JIA initiating MTX and a nested sub-cohort of 102 CYP with previously available baseline blood transcriptomic data were analysed. Clinical disease courses were classified using multivariate group-based trajectory modelling, while baseline interferon activity was quantified using established 51-gene and 5-gene expression signatures derived from bulk RNASeq. There was no association between pre-treatment 51-gene and 5-gene IFN response scores and distinct clinical disease trajectories following methotrexate initiation by regression modelling. Post-hoc calculations indicated that the study was underpowered (44-58%) to detect medium effects, demonstrating that the increased clinical resolution provided by trajectory analysis significantly compromises statistical power in size-limited paediatric cohorts. Clinical trajectories accurately describe patient heterogeneity, but the IFN score does not represent a marker for a specific trajectory group?. Future stratification strategies require larger multi-centre cohorts to identify non-responders early and exploit the window of biological opportunity.
